title: The Build Model: Declaration, Definition, Linker

questions.question: Building a C++ program takes two separate steps. What are they?
options: Checking syntax, then checking logic
Compiling, then running the tests
Downloading dependencies, then compiling
Compiling each source file, then linking the results into one program
questions.explanation: The compiler handles one translation unit at a time. The linker then connects every call to the code that implements it.

questions.question: What is the difference between a declaration and a definition?
options: A declaration is in a header, a definition is in a header too
There is no difference, the two words mean the same thing
A declaration promises a function exists, a definition supplies its body
A declaration is for variables, a definition is for functions
questions.explanation: A declaration gives the compiler the name and shape. A definition gives the actual code, and the linker needs exactly one of those.

questions.question: You see: undefined reference to celsius_from_raw(int). Which step failed?
options: Running, because the function crashed
Compiling, because the header was missing
Configuration, because CMake could not find the file
Linking, because no definition of that function was found
questions.explanation: The compiler accepted the call on the strength of the declaration. The linker then found no body to connect it to.

questions.question: Why do function bodies usually not belong in a header?
options: Headers are compiled more slowly than source files
Every file that includes it gets its own copy, so the linker sees duplicates
The compiler refuses to read function bodies in headers
Headers cannot contain more than one function
questions.explanation: Including a header copies its text in. If two translation units each get a definition, the linker reports a duplicate symbol, unless the function is marked inline.

questions.question: Why should is_overheating call celsius_from_raw instead of repeating 0.0625?
options: So a change to the sensor scale needs exactly one edit, not two
Because calling a function is faster than multiplying
Because the compiler cannot multiply inside a boolean function
Because repeating a number is a compile error
questions.explanation: Duplicated constants drift apart over time. One source of truth means one place to fix when the hardware changes.

questions.question: You define the same function in two .cpp files. What does the linker say?
options: Nothing, this is allowed
It reports an undefined reference
It reports a duplicate or multiple definition
It silently picks the first one
questions.explanation: The rule is exactly one definition. Zero gives an undefined reference, two or more gives a duplicate symbol.
